This suffers greatly from the curse of being the middle film in a trilogy, an adaptation of the middle volume of a single novel, content that would do fine as the second act of a single movie were this almost-ten-hour cinematic endeavour condensed into a less overwrought form, but struggles to function as a film in its own right when asked to stand alone in this manner. Gone is the first film's well-structured journey into fantastical realms of wonder, replaced by a lot of fairly dry political drama with the battle of Helm's Deep co-opted for the role of climactic spectacle to a three hour epic that covers surprisingly little narrative ground. Unfortunately, gone also is much of the visual prowess that made The Fellowship of the Ring noteworthy; New Zealand (the best part of the whole thing) is still beautiful of course, but the CGI feels like a less immersive step-down in quality, with locations we've seen already (e.g. Isengard) looking much less photoreal, the Ents being quite visually disappointing, and only the brief vision of the oliphaunts particularly gripping my imagination. The battle finale admittedly does its best to carry the film, and plays host to some epic moments (Legolas skateboarding down the stairway on a shield and Aragorn riding the falling ladder are hilariously awesome), but for my own taste it's not enough to save a film that I personally would not sit through again.

O Senhor dos Anéis: As Duas Torres assume a difícil missão de dar continuidade a uma trilogia épica dividindo o seu foco em múltiplas frentes narrativas. A grande virtude do filme está na sua impressionante escala de produção, destacando sequências de ação colossais que culminam na eletrizante Batalha do Abismo de Helm (uma aula de direção e efeitos práticos que continua impressionando pela grandiosidade técnica). Por outro lado, a estrutura fragmentada exigida pela adaptação literária acaba prejudicando bastante o ritmo da experiência. A narrativa se divide entre o núcleo de Rohan, a jornada de Frodo e Sam com Gollum e os passos de Merry e Pippin com os Ents, resultando em saltos constantes de tom e em momentos onde a trama simplesmente estagna (especialmente na lentidão arrastada das discussões dos Ents antes de decidirem agir). Apesar dos méritos técnicos inegáveis e da excelente construção do conflito político, o filme carrega o fardo clássico de ser a típica obra do meio que apenas prepara o terreno para o desfecho. É um espetáculo visualmente impecável, mas que peca por esticar excessivamente certas subtramas e perder parte do fôlego na transição entre os núcleos.

Watched the theatrical cut. Part I: This isn't awful, it's just incredibly, incredibly boring. The cgi effects and green screens are still dated, the colors still look awful, the comedy still doesn't work when it's attempted (God they made the comic relief dwarf SO much worse), and I just do not care about any of the characters old or new. It's better than Fellowship Part II in a technical sense but (and I can't believe I'm saying this) I am kind of missing it. Definitely the least eventful segment of the movies so far, I don't want to be a hater but I just really do not understand the love for it. Part II: Ugh. It gets like, maybe a tiny bit better? But not by much at all. More "events" happen, but none of this movie really feels important in the slightest. I do not care to see an army of orcs I don't care about battle a bunch of humans I don't care about. I'm all for political drama it has to be engaging on a character level and well-written, neither of which this is. It seems like this movie completely forgets its most interesting elements and cuts away from them for long segments at a time. Sam and Frodo are given almost nothing to do in this, and if you cut out all the battle fluff you're left with a pretty boring 45 minute short film (estimate). Fellowship, for all its flaws, had some sense of adventure to it, particularly in its first half - this does not. At all. I totally see why this movie seems to always be on cable television, because you really can and should just have it on in the background and not think about it too much. Probably the worst part is when they cut to Merry and Pippin, who spend most of their screentime riding on a poorly-animated tree which contributes literally nothing to the film until the last 20 minutes, when they can be used as more battle fodder. I just don't care. I don't care at all. This movie is not about the titular Two Towers, it isn't about Saruman, it isn't about the relationship between the two Hobbits Sam and Frodo on their massive and dangerous journey to destroy the most powerful item in the world. It's just about people that don't matter fighting, poorly-photographed and poorly-edited into an endless sea of grey and brown. In making the scale of the story so large, it completely fails to execute its underlying character arcs, and the world somehow only feels smaller and smaller than it did in the scenes (and film) prior. The whole "There's good in the world, Mr. Frodo" nonsense is so bs lol, they did not even try to develop that message throughout the rest of the movie and just completely shoehorned it in in the most obnoxiously unaware way possible. Maybe I'm too pessimistic, I'll give it another shot one day if I feel worthless and have 3 hours to spare, but it's getting a VERY light 3 out of me and nothing more. TLOTR writers room: Writer 1: Looks good! Cool fight scenes; Legolas looking into the distance saying some vague shit. It looks perfect! Wait, something's missing... Writer 2: Shit we forgot the tree subplot! Writer 1: Oh right, uhhh, just like weave it in between the exciting parts so that the audience keeps getting blue-balled. And make sure that each scene feels like absolutely nothing is progressing. You could argue it was a film technique to get the film ready for a grand ending, but I just ended up irritated. This one was definitely more engaging than the first film but keeps all the best parts of it and improves on some. More engaging character combinations and dialogue that let me feel the nature of their relationship with one another—namely Gimli, Legolas, Smeagol, and Gollum—unlike the very awkward Aragorn and Boromir scene towards the end of the first. Costumes, set, make-up, and overall mise en scene is still 10/10! Often, first movies in a trilogy will be very expository and lore-dumpy, then the second gets into the real action! One of the things I enjoyed was seeing how it pioneered action scenes in some of the most popular movies now in the way they were planned and choreographed. I could see what inspired Marvel movies like Avengers: Endgame (2019)'s final battle or The Lego Movie (2014)'s fight against the Kragle, I can appreciate the genius that inspired some of the greatest action and theatrical sequences put to screen. I'm not surprised that people in 2002 thought it was magnificent. But that's about it. I still care little for anyone and anything. They gave me more characters that flew from one ear and out the other. The elf dude that Aragorn hugged then died maybe 30 minutes later made me laugh, what was the point of that? The female "lead" is useless and I find the movie would be the same with or without her. When did making stories become about increasing your character count instead of using them as tools to tell a great narrative? But I'm not surprised by male fantasy pt. 2 disappointing me in that aspect. I'll be kind. It's the second movie. I expect all of these useless characters to become important later and I'll have to eat my sock. For now, it's a frustrating watch, but at least I wasn't dying of boredom thanks to those sick action scenes. Oh yeah and the tree subplot, kinda forgot to comment about it. Oh well, the film makers did too.

Por Guillermo Vaidovits (22 de diciembre de 2002) El 21 de diciembre del año pasado se estrenó en Guadalajara El señor de los anillos. Ahora llegó por las mismas fechas Las dos torres, cinta que prosigue las maravillosas aventuras de aquella. Dedicadas a su exhibición están 49 salas de las 158 que hay en la ciudad, prácticamente a donde se vaya topa uno con ella. Ninguna otra película en este año ha tenido semejante lanzamiento. Mi impresión general no la cambia esta nueva parte. Sigo pensando —y para decirlo tomo prestada una frase de Borges— "que su carencia de realidad sólo es comparable a su carencia, también desesperante, de irrealidad". Hay personajes que consiguen parecer de veras y otros sólo disfraces estrafalarios, pero en su totalidad se trata del repaso al catálogo completo de los héroes y villanos de las leyendas medievales, los mitos y los cuentos de hadas, juntos. Aunque más vivaz en esta ocasión —la verdad, sus tres horas pasan rápido— la película convence porque impone su tamaño antes que lo portentoso de sus hazañas. Si no se ha leído a Tolkien —carencia de la que me confieso feliz— o no se conoce la película anterior lo más seguro es que resulte complicado entender qué papel juega cada personaje e incluso la supuesta gravedad de lo que pasa. Al principio se presenta un resumen, pero eso solo sirve para llevarnos al punto donde arranca la acción. De todas maneras el centro del embrollo es muy sencillo: hay una sortija que es algo así como la fuente de poder de la malevolencia entera, unos hechiceros malos, malos, que la desean y un grupo de seres de diferentes clases (humanos, enanos de orejotas, elfos de orejas puntiagudas, hobbits, orcos) que intentan destruirla. Bueno, el caso es que en esta parte de la historia poco se afanan en resolver tal problema porque lo harán en la siguiente película y año. Las dos torres tiene la misión de servir de puente que lleve del segmento uno al tres. Gran número de muchachos y de aficionados a los libros de J. R. R. Tolkien proclaman que estas películas son lo más cercano que conocen a una obra maestra. Me temo que les ganan sus afectos. La película es entretenida y mucho más que la primera, pero no es mejor entretenimiento que otras de este año como El hombre araña o Camino a la perdición. La ventaja que le encuentro frente al común de las cintas comerciales es la manera en que, en algunos momentos, aprovecha la totalidad de la pantalla. En ese sentido se nota la preocupación del director por crear imágenes como grandes murales, en las que la vista pueda encontrar cosas interesantes aun en las esquinas y en los márgenes. Por televisión dichos cuidados pasarán inadvertidos.

Extended Edition Immer noch technisch gesehen unglaublich gut, aber emotional bekommt es mich einfach nicht. Ich bin an den Figuren und der Welt nicht wirklich interessiert. Ich glaube auch nicht, dass es an schlechtem Dialog, langweiligem Character Development oder Ähnlichem liegt, sondern eher daran, dass mich die Geschichte und die Fantasy-Welt nicht richtig catchen. Ich kann deshalb beide Seiten verstehen, sowohl Menschen bei denen LOTR überhaupt nicht funktioniert, als auch diejenigen, die es komplett glazen, so wie gefühlt 90 % der Leute (Bjarne). Ich glaube, das hängt hier wirklich stark von der jeweiligen Person ab und davon, wie sehr man sich auf diese Welt und ihre Geschichte einlassen kann. Was ich allerdings absolut anerkenne, ist, wie unglaublich viel handwerkliche Arbeit und Detailverliebtheit dahinterstecken.
